Even the ability to stand on an incline after a fall involves the ability to maintain single-limb stance. Individuals who demonstrate poor balance will exhibit inability to safely perform these activities.
The ability to perform and successfully maintain single-limb support for a specified amount of time can often determine where and how long we will live; with most falls resulting in significant injury to people over 50 years old.
In a recent article in Gerontology from March 2000 (Vol. 46: 90-93) the authors make note that the inability to maintain a simple one-leg stance in the elderly is as predictive of mortality risk as "the presence of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, or cognitive impairment."
The OLST requires the individual to stand on one foot (and remove support of the non-weight bearing foot) and maintain static balance for a specified length of time without touching the foot down.
In 1991, Westlake et al tested 100 healthy community-dwelling older adults and found a positive correlation between dynamic and static balance.2
The OLST is used as a functional test of postural control in the non-institutionalized geriatric population and is most appropriate for those who are considered community-dwelling and ambulatory.4

This practice of polychoral motets was especially popular during the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century. Claudio Monteverdi was the chief proponent of cor i spezzati, composing some forty works that utilized the style in his prime.
Long-standing tradition maintained that a group of musicians gathered in St. Mark's Cathedral in Venice (situated in the center of a group of islands in the eastern part of the country), around 1500, experimented with polychoral sound. Evidence to support this came from a sermon written in 1622 by a friar from the Church of San Silvestro of the Friars Minor in Venice, where it states: "And since the Cathedral was the first church in the world in which the manner of singing from more than one place, or corale, was invented, it should not be hidden that, in that same church, for many years there were as many as four coronae [choirs], from which voices rang out altogether when the singers rose from their seats."

Frequent flooding resulting from snow melt and rain on warmer winter days is another reality for tribes like the Karuk who depend on the river for fish and water flow. Unseasonably warm, dry weather like this one makes wildfires larger, causes extinction of salmon and other important fish species, and melts snow packs quickly, causing flash floods.
Faced with increasingly unpredictable weather and fewer fish, native peoples like the Karuk have been forced to find new ways of managing resources. The tribe’s Eco-Cultural Resources Management Plan is the manifestation of a long-standing need for adaptive management strategies for their environments.
Unlike Western sciences, which rely on tools such as satellites and ground radars to assess the physical condition of the Earth’s ecosystems, Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) is the process of gaining a holistic understanding of nature through observation and knowledge that is handed down through generations over centuries. Western sciences and TEK have different approaches to gathering information and analyzing resources, however both complement each other in their respective areas of expertise. The Karuk Tribe’s Eco-Cultural Resources Management Plan shows that more can be learned when the two are combined.
